structured_output.summary:
I found no direct CIFAR-100 evidence for most open hypotheses. Every speedrun result I found is on CIFAR-10. The airbench sources are the most useful.

1. **Muon (H1.2).** airbench94_muon is the current CIFAR-10 record. It drops the epoch count from 9.9 to 8 and FLOPs from 0.36 to 0.29 PFLOPs (about 19%), and time from 3.09 to 2.59 s (about 16%). Its settings: batch 2000, Muon lr 0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov, 3 Newton-Schulz steps; SGD momentum 0.85 for biases and the head; label smoothing 0.2. It drops lookahead entirely. That last point matters here, because E008 showed lookahead is worth about 1 pp in this CIFAR-100 regime. A Muon test should keep lookahead, or at least ablate it.

2. **Data selection (H1.4).** airbench96_faster cuts compute 37% (4.9 to 3.1 PFLOPs) and time 21% (34.7 to 27.3 s). It does this at about 37–45 epochs, using a 32/64/64, depth-2 proxy that keeps the hardest 512 of each 1024-example batch. Nothing I found shows it works around 9 epochs.

3. **Lookahead's value.** In the airbench paper's ablation, lookahead cut epochs from 13.5 to 12.0 (about 11%) on CIFAR-10. E008 found it worth about 2–3 times more on CIFAR-100, so tuning its schedule is a gap in the tree.

4. **Hiverge's 1.99 s CIFAR-10 record.** Untried levers: SiLU instead of GELU (relevant to the memory-bound elementwise kernels at about 18% of GPU time), random brightness/contrast augmentation, and whitening fit by SVD instead of eigendecomposition.

5. **Reference points.**
   - The full-length airbench96 recipe (37 epochs, cutout 12, translate 4) reaches 79.3–79.8% on CIFAR-100.
   - A public team recipe adapted from airbench reports 75.29% in 8.11 s on an A100-SXM4-80GB. That is below this task's 0.753 bar and about equal to the current tip (8.09 s, 0.7551). I couldn't read it: the PR page returned 404.

6. **Progressive resizing (H2.3).** Only generic support. MosaicML's guidance is to use crop mode (not resize) for CIFAR, start at scale 0.5 for the first 50% of training, and finish the last 20% at full size. I found no airbench-scale measurements.

findings.claim: airbench94_muon reaches 94.01% on CIFAR-10 (n=200) in 2.59 s using 0.29 PFLOPs. airbench94_compiled (SGD plus lookahead) needs 3.09 s and 0.36 PFLOPs, so Muon saves about 19% of FLOPs and about 16% of wall-clock. Muon recipe: batch size 2000, 8 epochs, Muon on 4D conv filters (flattened with reshape(len(g), -1)), lr 0.24, momentum 0.6, Nesterov, 3 Newton-Schulz iterations with coefficients (3.4445, -4.7750, 2.0315). Nesterov SGD (momentum 0.85) for the whitening bias (lr 0.053, trained for 3 epochs only) and the head (lr 0.67). Weight decay 2e-6 x batch size, label smoothing 0.2, linear decay to zero, widths 64/256/256, BatchNorm momentum 0.6, NO lookahead or EMA.
findings.relevance: This is the only quantitative evidence for H1.2/H1.2.1. On CIFAR-10, Muon gives about 16-19% at 94%. But the Muon recipe drops lookahead, and E008 showed lookahead is worth about 1 pp (1-2 epochs) on CIFAR-100 at 9 epochs. A faithful port without lookahead may therefore lose more than Muon gains. Test Muon with lookahead kept. Muon's lr/momentum were tuned for widths 64/256/256 and batch 2000, so 128/384/576 may need retuning.

findings.claim: Muon cut the CIFAR-10 94% record from 3.3 to 2.6 A100-seconds. Nesterov momentum worked better than plain SGD momentum in every case tested. Conv filters are handled by flattening their last three dimensions. The FLOP overhead is about T*m/B, which is under 1% in typical settings. Input/output layers and scalar or vector parameters should use a standard optimizer.
findings.relevance: The Newton-Schulz overhead on the 128/384/576 conv filters should be negligible compared with the roughly 19 ms GPU-bound step. Any H1.2 test is a sample-efficiency question, not a systems one.

findings.claim: airbench96_faster hits 96.00% on CIFAR-10 (n=200) in 27.3 s using 3.1 PFLOPs, against 34.7 s and 4.9 PFLOPs for airbench96. That is -21% time and -37% FLOPs. A proxy net (widths 32/64/64, depth 2) scores every 1024-example batch, and only the 512 highest-loss examples get the main model's backward pass. Both run for about 40 epochs, with lookahead and TTA level 2.
findings.relevance: Data selection works at airbench96 scale. But that regime trains about 4x longer, and its proxy costs a full proxy training pass. At about 9 epochs the main model still underfits, so per-batch selection may cost accuracy. Treat H1.4.1 as low-prior. A cheaper variant is to compute losses from the main model's own forward pass, which drops the separate proxy.

findings.claim: Ablation steps to reach 94% on CIFAR-10: patch-whitening gives 21 epochs (8.0 s), dirac init 18 epochs (6.8 s), BatchNorm-bias scaling 13.5 epochs (5.1 s), lookahead 12.0 epochs (4.6 s). So lookahead saved about 11% of epochs. Alternating flip gave a 27.1% effective speedup over random flip, for airbench94 without TTA at 20 epochs. Without TTA, airbench94/95/96 reach 93.2/94.4/95.6% (TTA is worth about 0.4-0.8 pp). On CIFAR-100, airbench96 gets 79.27% without cutout and 79.76% with it, versus ResNet-18 at 77.54/78.04%.
findings.relevance: E008 measured lookahead at about 1 pp (1-2 epochs) on CIFAR-100, larger than the 11% it bought on CIFAR-10. Weight averaging matters more here. Its schedule (decay 0.95^5 * (t/T)^3 every 5 steps) was tuned for CIFAR-10 and is a promising lever the tree has not covered (proposed new H4.2.x). The TTA gap of about 0.4-0.8 pp agrees with E006's finding that TTA is worth about 0.5-1 epoch.

findings.claim: airbench96 settings: 37 epochs, batch 1024, lr 9.0, momentum 0.85, decoupled weight decay 0.012, label smoothing 0.2, widths 128/384/512, 3 convs per group, residual connections in the later conv layers. Augmentation is cutout 12 plus translate 4 with alternating flip. BatchNorm has no learnable weight, only a bias, with eps=1e-12. BatchNorm-bias lr x64, whitening bias trained for 3 epochs then frozen, lookahead decay 0.95^5*(step/T)^3, TTA level 2. Result: 96.03% in 34.7 s on an A100-SXM4-80GB.
findings.relevance: The arena recipe uses translate-2 with no cutout and 9 epochs. Cutout and translate-4 are tuned for 37 epochs and would likely hurt at 9. Note that airbench96 uses label smoothing 0.2, consistent with E004 (0.2 is about equal to 0.3). If the arena net lacks airbench96's residual connections in the later groups, check whether adding them changes accuracy at 9 epochs.

findings.claim: The Hiverge CIFAR-10 record (1.99 s on A100, 94%, previously 2.59 s) used a vectorized Muon (matrices padded and batched into one bmm), vectorized augmentation, random brightness/contrast augmentation, confidence-gated selective TTA, SiLU instead of GELU, whitening initialized by SVD instead of eigendecomposition, and a compiled forward+backward. It also retuned steps, lr, momentum, dtypes and memory formats. No CIFAR-100 results.
findings.relevance: TTA is forbidden here, and E005 refuted the compiled step plus fused optimizer for SGD. Two untested ideas remain. (a) SiLU in place of GELU: the fused BN/GELU elementwise kernels are about 18% of GPU time, and SiLU's forward and backward are cheaper. Accuracy needs checking. (b) Brightness/contrast augmentation as a cheap GPU op that might add accuracy per epoch. If Muon is adopted (H1.2), a batched Newton-Schulz across same-shape conv filters is the matching systems trick.

findings.claim: A public CIFAR-100 speedrun PR is titled 'Modal runner and recipe (75.29% in 8.11 s, baseline 59.3 s)', with the recipe adapted from airbench. Search snippets say it ran on a Modal A100-SXM4-80GB.
findings.relevance: This is the only external CIFAR-100 reference point. The arena tip (E010: 0.7551 at 8.09 s) matches its time while keeping the margin that 75.29% would miss under the 0.753 bar. Nothing public seems to be well ahead of the tip, so further gains must come from new levers (Muon, lookahead tuning, SiLU), not from copying.

findings.claim: The organizer repo's verified baseline (2026-10-02) is ResNet9, width 64, 40 epochs: 75.36% mean accuracy (2 trials), 59.30 s mean prepare+train, 0.117 s inference, on an A100 80GB PCIe. The rules require 40 seeds and a mean of 75% or more, with no per-trial floor. Some search snippets describe an older version judged on an L40S with 50 trials.
findings.relevance: Confirms the official target and hardware. The judging GPU is the PCIe A100, which has lower power/clock limits than the SXM4. The ~1-3% systems gains should carry over, but absolute times will differ. No public leaderboard submissions are visible.

findings.claim: MosaicML recommends initial_scale 0.5, delay_fraction 0.5, finetune_fraction 0.2 (final 20% at full size) and size_increment 4. Crop mode worked better than resize for ResNet-56 on CIFAR-10. Lower accuracy per step is offset by more steps per wall-clock second.
findings.relevance: Weak, generic support for H2.3. For CIFAR, use crop mode (24 px crops early), not downsampling. With frozen 2x2 patch-whitening and global max-pool, the net handles 24 px input. The extra compiled shapes must be warmed up in build(). There is no airbench-scale evidence, and early low-res epochs may conflict with the steep accuracy-vs-epoch curve below 9 epochs seen in E006.

findings.claim: A critically damped momentum schedule mu(t)=1-2*sqrt(alpha(t)) gives 2-4x early speedups on CIFAR-100 (ResNet-18/VGG-16, 5 seeds). The final accuracy cost grows to 1.7 pp, so the accuracy-matched gain shrinks to 1.14x. A hybrid that switches to mu=0.9 near the end recovers the final accuracy on CIFAR-10.
findings.relevance: Momentum schedules are a lever the tree hasn't covered. The evidence comes from long ResNet runs, and the end-of-training gain is small (1.14x), so it is a low-prior side direction for the 9-epoch regime. Retuning momentum (0.85 now) together with the lookahead schedule is more promising.
